domains.title: Island of the Eighty-Eight Temples
domains.subtitle: Pilgrimage, Rural Japan, and the Cult of Kūkai
domains.lead: Shikoku is Japan's smallest main island, a place of mountains, coast, and rural quiet. For more than a thousand years it has been walked by pilgrims on the henro, the 88-temple circuit associated with Kūkai, the founder of Shingon Buddhism. Shikoku means 'four provinces,' and its identity is inseparable from the spiritual geography of the pilgrimage.

cards.name: Shikoku Henro
cards.desc: The 88-temple pilgrimage circuit honoring Kūkai; in Shingon numerology the 88 stands for the bonnō, the delusions each temple is walked to release.

cards.name: Kūkai's Island
cards.desc: The birthplace and spiritual home of the Shingon founder, born at Zentsū-ji in Sanuki in 774.

cards.name: Mountain Asceticism
cards.desc: Ishizuchi-san and ridges like Yokomine-ji (temple 60) preserve the Shugendō layer beneath the Buddhist circuit.

cards.name: Four Provinces
cards.desc: Awa, Tosa, Iyo, and Sanuki — the ancient kuni that gave the island its name and that the pilgrimage stitches into one body.

symbols.name: Pilgrim's staff and sedge hat
symbols.meaning: The kongō-zue staff rings for the dead who walk with the henro, and the sugegasa shades the white-robed pilgrim.

symbols.name: Osettai
symbols.meaning: The free food, lodging, and small gifts islanders offer walkers — the gift economy that sustains the circuit.

symbols.name: Eighty-eight temples
symbols.meaning: The sacred circuit that defines Shikoku's spiritual geography, one temple for each of the bonnō.

symbols.name: Naruto whirlpools
symbols.meaning: The famous tidal whirlpools at the island's eastern edge, where the Seto Inland Sea meets the Pacific.

symbols.name: The white robe (byakue)
symbols.meaning: The pilgrim's garment, worn as a funeral shroud for the self — the walker dies to ordinary life at temple one.

mythology.lead: Shikoku's mythology is the mythology of Kūkai and the Buddhist pilgrimage that bears his memory — documented history, medieval hagiography, and mountain legend fused into a single sacred geography that thousands of pilgrims in white still walk each year, temple by temple, around the island.

myths.title: Kūkai: The Boy of Zentsū-ji
myths.text: Kūkai (774–835), later venerated as Kōbō Daishi, was born in the village of Byōbugaura in Sanuki province — present-day Zentsū-ji city, where temple 75 still marks the family home. The medieval biographies wrap his life in marvel: as a youth he was sent by a despairing kinsman into the mountain wilderness, and there, tradition says, the esoteric teachings came to him in visionary form. The documentary core is solid: in 804 he sailed to Tang China, studied Sanskrit and esoteric Buddhism at the Qinglong monastery in Chang'an under the Indian master Huiguo, returned in 806 laden with scriptures and ritual implements, founded the Shingon school, and in 816 received imperial leave to open a mountain monastery on Kōya-san. His own early writings — the Sango Shiiki of 797 and the Shōrai Mokuroku of 806 — are among the founding documents of Japanese Buddhist literature. When he died on Kōya-san in 835, tradition refused the word: the master had entered eternal samādhi in the Okunoin and would sit there until the coming of the future Buddha. The hagiography makes the point the pilgrims still act on: on Shikoku, Kūkai never left.

myths.title: The Eighty-Eight Temples and the Companion Beside You
myths.text: The Shikoku Henro links 88 temples in a circuit of some 1,200 kilometres, and the number is itself theology: in Shingon numerology there are eighty-eight bonnō, the delusions that bind the heart, and each temple is understood to release one. The circuit as pilgrims walk it took shape in the Edo period, when temple associations, printed guidebooks such as the Shikoku Reijōki, and the island-wide institution of osettai — free food and lodging offered to walkers — made the henro a mass practice. Pilgrims wear the white byakue and sugegasa hat and carry a kongō-zue staff whose metal rings announce the dead traveling with them, and they address the Daishi not as a memory but as a companion: the walk's first principle is dōgyō ninin, 'two traveling together' — yourself and Kūkai. Walking tales insist the Daishi appears along the road as a child, a beggar, or a stranger who vanishes around the bend. The circuit turns a whole island into one ritual body: to walk Shikoku is to walk through Kūkai's biography, one delusion at a time.

myths.title: En no Gyōja and the Peaks of Ishizuchi
myths.text: Long before the eighty-eight temples were numbered, Shikoku's mountains were training grounds. The great peak Ishizuchi-san (1,982 m) in Ehime is a principal center of Shugendō, the mountain-ascetic tradition, and its founding legend belongs to En no Gyōja — the seventh-century wonder-working ascetic whom the court exiled and who, tradition says, flew over the capital and tamed demons into Buddhism. Shugendō communities hold that En trained on Ishizuchi and sealed its mountain spirits; the summit still keeps a shrine to the Tengu, the red-faced spirit who tested and then served him, and ascetic rites continue there in season. Several henro temples preserve the same mountain character — none more than Yokomine-ji, temple 60, which clings to a ridge at seven hundred metres and was rebuilt from near-abandonment in the 1970s by its yamabushi community. The island's sacred geography thus runs on two engines: Kūkai's circuit below and En's peaks above, the walking pilgrimage and the climbing one.

myths.title: Four Provinces and the Man Who Moved the World
myths.text: Shikoku — literally 'four countries' — is an island the ancient state made: the ritsuryō provincial reforms of the seventh century carved it into Awa, Tosa, Iyo, and Sanuki, the four kuni that gave the island its name and that the pilgrimage later stitched back into a single sacred circuit. For most of its history the island was a maritime world of fishing ports, steep fields, and castle towns — Tokushima, Kōchi, Matsuyama, Takamatsu — reachable from the mainland only by sea. In the nineteenth century one Shikoku son helped end the age he was born into: Sakamoto Ryōma (1836–1867), a low-ranking samurai of the Tosa domain, brokered the secret alliance of Satsuma and Chōshū against the shōgunate and sketched a Japan governed by councils of daimyō and court nobles rather than by a military dictator — a vision he lived just long enough to see begun. The island's modern identity holds both halves at once: the henro's slow walking world, and the Tosa-born revolutionary who could not wait for it.

lore.syncretism: Shikoku's religious landscape is layered rather than replaced. Buddhist temples and Shinto shrines share precincts along the henro, and the island's kami — the mountain powers of Ishizuchi, the sea deities of the whirlpool coast — are read through the honji-suijaku logic as local manifestations of buddhas and bodhisattvas. The pilgrimage itself absorbed folk religion: osettai is a village institution older than any temple guild, and the Daishi is at once a historical monk, an incarnation of a cosmic buddha, and a helpful stranger on the road. In the modern era the henro has been recast for international walkers, secular hikers, and 'power spot' tourists without losing its ritual grammar, and churches and new religions appear among the givers of osettai. Syncretism here is not a single historical event but the island's permanent condition: every age walks the same road and calls the companion by a different name.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Shikoku Henro remains one of Japan's most important pilgrimages, walked by tens of thousands each year — on foot, by bus, in section over a lifetime — and studied worldwide as a model of living religious practice (Statler, Japanese Pilgrimage, 1983; Reader & Tanabe, Practically Religious, 1998). The island's rural culture, its udon, its vine bridges and thatched Iya villages are celebrated as the 'hidden Japan' of slow travel. Kūkai's bequest runs beyond religion: tradition credits him with perfecting the kana syllabaries and founding Japan's first school open to commoners, and the Daishi's name opens esoteric rites across the country. Shikoku has become the national emblem of a counter-rhythm — the island where the answer to speed is not nostalgia but a walking staff.
lore.extendedMeditation: Shikoku teaches that a place can become sacred through walking. The island is not merely the setting of the pilgrimage; the pilgrimage is the island's true form. Every mountain pass, fishing hamlet, and henro trail between the temples is part of the rite, and the islanders' osettai makes the whole population liturgists. To walk the henro is to let the land shape the soul at walking pace — the pace at which things actually change. The circuit also makes an audacious claim about numbers: eighty-eight is not a route length but a diagnosis, one temple for each delusion of the human heart. You do not walk the island to see Kūkai's sites; you walk it so that the walking, repeated daily for weeks, wears the self down to something lighter. In an age of acceleration, Shikoku's quiet insistence is that the shortest distance to the sacred is the long way round.

lore.archaeology: The material record of the island's sacred culture is continuous and visible. Zentsū-ji (temple 75) preserves the Kūkai birth precinct, the Miedō hall with the birth room still shown to pilgrims, and Tairyū-ji (temple 21) on its eastern ridge guards the vajra said to have flown there when the young Kūkai prayed for a sign. Henro temples from Ryōzen-ji (temple 1, early 9th c.) onward preserve Daishi halls where food is offered daily to Kūkai as one still present — because he is believed to be. On Ishizuchi-san, the summit shrine and the chained final ascent mark the Shugendō layer of the cult. Across the water, the Okunoin of Kōya-san — Kūkai's mausoleum, part of the UNESCO World Heritage 'Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range' (2004) — is the circuit's gravitational center, where the lanterns before the master are said to have burned for twelve centuries.
lore.cult:
The henro is a liturgy in hiking boots. At each of the eighty-eight temples the pilgrim performs the same compact rite: bow at the gate, wash, ring the temple bell, light incense, and chant the Heart Sutra before the main image — then turn to the Daishi hall and recite the mantra Namu Daishi Henjō Kongō, 'homage to the Daishi, whose illumination is the vajra,' because Kōbō Daishi is present, not remembered. The nōkyōchō stamp book and the osame-fuda name slip carry the proof of each visit, and the rings of the white staff announce the dead walking beside.

The deepest cult act happens off the island. At the Okunoin on Kōya-san the monks still carry meals to Kūkai's tomb twice a day, twelve centuries on, setting food before a master who is believed to be meditating, not gone. Shikoku's islanders complete the rite from the other side with osettai, the gifts of food and lodging that make every walker a walking altar and every doorstep a chapel.
lore.iconography:
Shikoku's sacred images are portraits and waymarks. The supreme likeness is a monk's face: tradition credits the disciple Shin'nyo with a painting of Kūkai made from life, preserved on Kōya-san as the sacred image of the Miedō, and the gentle, round-cheeked master in travelling robe, vajra and rosary in hand, descends from it in every Daishi hall on the circuit.

The walking image is older than any statue: pilgrims read the island itself as his body, and early modern Japan printed it — the Edo-period guidebooks and pilgrimage mandalas compress the whole circuit, temples, coasts, and mountains, into a single sacred diagram. On the route the Daishi stands in bronze or stone at nearly every temple gate, straw-sandalled and staff in hand, and small anonymous figures appear at the roadside too, since the road's first principle is that he may be anyone you meet. Ishizuchi-san's chained summit shrine and its tengu images mark the older Shugendō layer above the circuit.
lore.reception:
The transmission of Kūkai's Shikoku runs from hagiography to hiking boot. Medieval compilations of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries fixed the wonder-filled biography pilgrims still carry — the boy of Zentsū-ji, the voyage to Chang'an, the master who would not die — and Edo-period printing turned the circuit into a mass institution with guidebooks, temple guilds, and the osettai village network that still feeds walkers.

The modern era first thinned the roads, then made the pilgrimage famous abroad: Oliver Statler walked it and wrote Japanese Pilgrimage (1983), the book that carried the henro to Anglophone readers, and Reader and Tanabe's Practically Religious (1998) made it the textbook case of religion practiced for worldly benefit. In Japan the circuit recovered as the nation's counter-rhythm, walked by tens of thousands each year — on foot, by bus, a few temples a year for a lifetime — and the Shugendō rites on Ishizuchi were re-founded after near-abandonment in the 1970s. What the Middle Ages made legend and the Edo age made infrastructure, the twentieth century made literature; the walk itself continues.
